readerTitle: Why the simpler quote wins the job
caseNote: 가상 사례 (청소 서비스, 카페 소모품 유통) + 실제 기업의 일반적 특징 (Aldi의 짧은 상품 구성)
insight: 단순함은 기능이 없는 상태가 아니라 고객이 할 일을 줄여 주는 기능이며, 대개 그 복잡함을 회사가 대신 떠안아야 만들어진다.
misconception: 선택지와 옵션을 많이 줄수록 더 많은 고객이 자기에게 맞는 것을 찾아서 산다. 단순하게 만들면 비용이 줄어든다.

sources.text: Aldi 공식 자료 및 언론 보도: 일반 슈퍼마켓보다 훨씬 적은 품목 수와 높은 자체 브랜드 비중
청소 서비스와 카페 소모품 유통 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Aldi가 일반 슈퍼마켓보다 훨씬 적은 품목을 취급하고, 품목당 한두 가지 버전만 두며, 자체 브랜드 비중이 높다는 점을 게시 전 Aldi 공식 자료로 확인하세요. 구체적 품목 수는 나라와 시기마다 달라 카드에 숫자를 쓰지 않았습니다.
짧은 상품 구성이 구매·진열·재고 운영을 단순하게 해 낮은 가격에 도움이 된다는 설명은 일반적으로 알려진 분석입니다. 표현이 과장되지 않았는지 확인하세요.
청소 견적($160, 추가 옵션 24개), 카페 80곳, 300개 품목 가격표는 모두 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 계산이 필요한 숫자는 없습니다.

cards.title: Two cleaning quotes land in the same inbox.
body: One lists a base price plus 24 optional extras, from inside-oven cleaning to blind dusting. The other says: *$160 for a two-bedroom home, everything included.*
The first looks cheaper on paper. The customer books the second, and doesn't even read the first one to the end.

image.label: A long itemized quote next to a one-line quote
image.brief: 휴대폰 화면 두 개를 나란히. 왼쪽은 체크박스가 빽빽한 긴 견적서가 화면 밖까지 이어지고, 오른쪽은 큰 글씨로 "$160, everything included" 한 줄과 "Book" 버튼. 오른쪽에 엄지손가락이 닿는 모습. 실제 회사 로고 없음.

cards.title: Lots of quotes, few bookings.
body: You run a home-cleaning company. Many people request a quote, but most never book. Your quote is a base price plus a long list of add-ons.

options.text: Add more add-ons, so every customer finds exactly what they need
options.feedback: You gain a closer fit for some customers. But every extra line is another decision, and another reason to wonder what the final bill will be.
A lower price may lift bookings a little, but it costs you margin and leaves the confusing quote in place.

options.text: Replace the list with one flat price by home size, common extras included
options.feedback: The customer can say yes in seconds. In return, you take on the work of pricing an average job. The next cards explain why that trade works.

cards.title: The long quote gave the customer a job.
body: An itemized quote turns the customer into a project manager. They must guess which extras they need, add up the total, and worry that the real bill will be higher.
The flat price removes all three tasks. Nothing was added to the cleaning itself. **Something was removed from the customer's work**, and that was what they were buying.

cards.title: Simplicity as a feature
body: **Simplicity** is the effort a customer saves in understanding, choosing and using what you sell.

Treat it as a feature: something you design, test and protect, the same way you treat quality or speed. It isn't the same as having fewer things. It's about how little the customer has to think before saying yes.

image.label: A customer's path from many steps to a few
image.brief: 고객이 걷는 길 두 개를 비교하는 인포그래픽. 위쪽 길은 "Compare", "Add up", "Guess", "Worry" 표지판이 많고 구불구불함. 아래쪽 길은 짧고 곧으며 끝에 "Done". 플랫한 일러스트 스타일.

cards.softwareNote: In software, simplicity often means sensible default settings, one clear price plan, or a signup that asks three questions instead of twenty. Users rarely praise it, but they notice fast when it's missing.

cards.title: Someone still carries the complexity.
body: Simple for the customer usually means more work for you. The flat-price cleaner has to estimate the average job, train crews to handle surprises, and accept that some homes will take longer than planned.
The complexity didn't disappear. It moved from the customer's head to the business's planning.
cards.callout: Simplicity isn't free. You buy it on the customer's behalf.

cards.title: A grocer that sells less on purpose.
body: Discount grocers such as Aldi carry a much shorter range than a typical supermarket, often just one or two versions of each product, many under their own label.

Shoppers give up some choice. In return, the trip is quicker and each decision is easier. The short range also makes buying, shelving and stock simpler for the grocer, which helps keep prices low. **Simplicity here is part of the offer**, not a gap in it.

image.label: A short, tidy shelf beside a crowded one
image.brief: 마트 진열대 두 개 비교. 왼쪽은 같은 상품의 다양한 버전이 빽빽이 쌓여 있고, 오른쪽은 품목마다 한두 가지만 정돈되어 있으며 쇼핑객이 빠르게 집어 감. 실제 상표나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Simple still has to do the job.
body: If the flat price leaves out what customers actually need, they feel cheated, not relieved. Simplicity only works when the core is right.
Some customers want control. An experienced buyer may prefer the full catalog to your curated kit, so know who you're simplifying for.
And simplicity wears away. Each exception you add for one customer makes the offer a little harder for the next.

cards.title: Now you're a supplier.
body: You supply cleaning products and paper goods to 80 small cafés. Ordering means a 300-line price list and a phone call each week. Cafés often run out, then rush-order.

options.text: Add more products, so cafés can get everything from you
options.feedback: You might win a bigger share of each order, but busy owners now face an even longer list. The ordering problem gets worse.

options.text: Give each café a standing weekly order, based on past orders, that they confirm or adjust with one reply
options.feedback: The café's weekly decision shrinks to "yes" or a small change. You take on the work of tracking usage, and you likely get steadier orders.

options.text: Offer 5% off orders placed by Monday
options.feedback: This rewards planning ahead, but the café still has to read the list and do the planning. You pay for the discount without removing the work.

cards.title: Make the customer's job smaller.
body: Simplicity is a feature you build by taking work off the customer, often by taking it on yourself.
**Try it today:** walk through buying from you as a brand-new customer. Count every decision they have to make. Pick one you could make for them.
